# On Noticing Things

There's a particular pleasure in noticing a pattern you weren't looking for. You're reading something mundane—a grocery list, a weather report—and suddenly you see that the words on the page echo something from a conversation last week, or that two unrelated facts you've been carrying around separately suddenly click together into a single shape. Nobody assigned you this connection. It wasn't on a syllabus. It just arrived, unbidden, because some part of the mind keeps working in the background, sorting and re-sorting, long after you've stopped paying conscious attention.

I think a lot about the architecture of attention—not in a clinical sense, but in the way it shapes what becomes possible for a person to think. Attention is selective by necessity; if you tried to give full weight to every stimulus reaching you at once, you'd be paralyzed, or worse, dissolved into noise. So the mind builds filters. It decides, mostly without consulting you, what counts as signal and what counts as static. The strange part is that these filters aren't neutral. They're built from history—your history, your culture's history, the accidents of what you happened to be taught to value. Two people can stand in the same room and see entirely different rooms, because their filters have trained them to notice different furniture.

This is part of why conversation is so strange and so valuable. When you talk to someone genuinely different from you—different background, different training, different obsessions—you're not just exchanging facts. You're temporarily borrowing their filter. You get to see, for a moment, what the room looks like when furnished by a different set of habits. This is, I think, the actual mechanism behind the cliché that travel "broadens the mind." It's not the airports or the unfamiliar food. It's the forced encounter with a different filter, one that makes visible all the choices your own filter has been making invisibly, your whole life, without your permission.

Language is the most interesting filter of all, because it's the one we use to describe the other filters. Every language carves the world up differently—not just into different words, but into different categories of thing worth having a word for. Some languages have a single word for what English needs a paragraph to express; others make distinctions English speakers don't even notice are missing. This isn't a parlor trick. It shapes what's easy to think and what's hard to think, what comes up as an option to consider and what stays invisible because there was never a hook to hang it on.

And yet language is also wonderfully leaky. People constantly say things they don't quite have words for, gesturing at a feeling or an idea with metaphor, with comparison, with a kind of pointing-toward that doesn't require precision. "It's like trying to hold water" gets at something that no single word for frustration quite captures. This is maybe the most human thing about language: not its precision, but its capacity to be stretched toward meanings it wasn't originally built to carry. We're constantly repurposing old words for new uses, the way you might use a coffee mug as a pencil holder—not because it was designed for that, but because it happens to work, and the workaround becomes, eventually, just another ordinary use.

I find myself drawn, too, to the question of what makes something memorable versus what gets erased entirely. Most of what happens to a person in a day doesn't survive past the day itself. It's not stored, not really, except maybe as a vague residue, a slight shift in mood with no clear cause. But certain things stick—not always the important things, often the strange small ones. The exact color of light in a room during a particular conversation. A stranger's odd phrase, overheard and never explained. There's no good theory, as far as I know, that fully predicts what gets kept and what gets dropped. Memory seems to have its own taste, separate from the taste of the conscious mind, and it doesn't always consult you before deciding what's worth keeping.

Maybe this is connected to why certain ideas feel important even when you can't yet justify why. Intuition might just be memory's filing system surfacing a connection before the conscious, verbal part of you has caught up enough to explain it. You feel that something matters before you can say why it matters, and the saying-why often comes later, sometimes much later, sometimes not at all. There's a temptation to distrust this—to insist that nothing counts until it can be fully articulated—but I think that's a mistake. Some of the best thinking starts as an itch, a hunch, a sense that there's something here worth turning over, long before there's an argument to defend it.

If I had to name a single thread running through all of this, it would be a kind of faith in the unfinished. Filters keep changing. Languages keep stretching to cover new ground. Memory keeps surprising you with what it decided to keep. None of it arrives as a finished system, fully justified and locked into place. It's always provisional, always being revised by the next conversation, the next piece of unexpected information, the next quiet noticing of a pattern nobody assigned you to find. That provisionality used to seem, to me, like a weakness—proof that nothing can be trusted because everything is subject to revision. Now it seems more like the whole point. A mind that couldn't be revised wouldn't be thinking. It would just be repeating.
